title: Laser Weapons Are Finally Going to War: The US Military Has Already Spent $15 Billion on R&D
dek: Lasers are called the sniper rifles of directed energy weapons, while microwaves are the electronic shotgun. The US military is shifting from R&D to procurement, but the real shortage is cheap interceptors—can you win every engagement but still lose the war because you can't afford it?
why: This episode explains the real bottlenecks of laser weapons from physics principles and operational economics, also touching on supply chains and the defense procurement landscape. It's for anyone interested in defense tech and defense stocks.
who: Defense industry analysts, defense tech VCs, readers following China's military modernization, and anyone trying to understand the US military's ammunition consumption anxiety.
skip: The first few minutes of event promo and small talk can be skipped to 05:08 where the guest's military background is introduced.

points.h: Lasers are sniper rifles, microwaves are shotguns
points.body: Wayne uses the analogy that lasers are sniper rifles and microwaves are electronic shotguns to distinguish the two types of directed energy weapons: lasers concentrate energy into a narrow beam, engaging one target at a time and burning through it with heat; microwaves have a wider beam and can affect the electronics of multiple targets simultaneously. The Government Accountability Office notes that high-power microwaves can reach peak powers of 100 megawatts, but comparing that directly to the kilowatts of continuous-wave lasers is meaningless because the two are fundamentally different: lasers try to increase power, microwaves try to amplify area effects. The choice depends on the target—drone swarms are suited to microwaves, while a single ballistic missile can only be engaged by a laser. This is because microwaves can disable drones and make them fall, but unlike lasers, they cannot destroy a single high-speed missile.

points.h: Chemical lasers failed on size and logistics
points.body: After the laser was invented in the 1960s, the military immediately saw its potential, but the real problems were power and size. In the 1990s, the US-Israeli Tactical High Energy Laser and DARPA's MIRACLE chemical laser both successfully shot down rockets, but the systems were huge and logistically complex, leading to program termination in 2006. Chemical lasers get light energy directly from chemical reactions and don't need electricity—for example, the oxygen-iodine laser was mounted on a Boeing 747 (YAL-1) to try to intercept ballistic missiles near their launch area, but carrying chemicals on an aircraft was too dangerous. Today's key metric for technological progress is SWaP: size, weight, and power. In the past, lasers were as big as a building because they required enormous amounts of electricity to generate the beam, whereas today the goal is to fit them on trucks and warships.

points.h: Handheld laser bottleneck is power compression
points.body: When asked why sci-fi handheld laser guns don't exist yet, Wayne points to the bottleneck of 'power generation and compression.' The fastest land platform currently is a high-energy laser mounted on a Stryker armored vehicle, with 50 kilowatts of power, relying on the vehicle's own generation. If you need a 5-kilowatt beam to shoot down a drone, you might need 15 to 25 kilowatts of input power; without sufficient power, you can only watch drones fly toward you with no way to respond. Electricity is the core constraint, not a gap in optical technology. This also explains why laser weapons have been in development for decades and are only now approaching the tipping point for large-scale deployment.

Many people think lasers can replace multi-million-dollar interceptor missiles, but Wayne warns that if the enemy launches a hypersonic weapon, you wouldn't want to gamble on a laser hitting a Mach 5 target precisely. So the real framework is 'integrated air and missile defense'—a combination of layered defenses. Lasers and microwaves have the advantage of low cost per shot, but you have to wait for the target to get close enough to be engaged; against weapons traveling at 4,000 miles per hour, you still need carefully designed interceptors like PAC-3 and SM-3. Israel is the best example: Arrow 2/3 for long-range ballistic missiles, David's Sling for medium range, Iron Dome for rockets, and now Iron Beam for drones.

points.h: Battlefield commanders don't care about unit cost
points.body: When asked who thinks about cost when opening fire, Wayne divides decision-making into four levels: tactical, operational, strategic, and national. A frontline platoon or company commander facing a threat will use whatever means necessary to protect troops, not caring about the missile's price; but at the theater commander and Pentagon level, you have to consider whether it's worth using a $4.1 million PAC-3 to shoot down a $30,000 drone. So the demand for 'cheap weapons' comes from the top, not the bottom. Only national-level decision-makers factor ammunition consumption and supply chain into the choice. This distinction explains why the US military, after being attrited in Yemen and the Red Sea, is shifting toward low-cost interception solutions.

points.h: US military pivots to low-cost munitions
points.body: Over the past decades, the US military has stockpiled more and more expensive precision interceptors for high-end peer warfare, only to be forced to change by drones in Yemen and the Red Sea. Wayne says the Pentagon is signing multi-year framework agreements to significantly increase production, but the core realization is that you can't always use expensive solutions against cheap threats. His key judgment: in future conflicts, 'you can win every engagement but still lose the war economically.' This is the market demand for low-cost interceptors like Coyote, Vampire, and APKWS. Battlefield commanders need more options at hand, not just the ability to fire off expensive missiles.

When asked whether laser weapons might be stifled by defense giants due to the innovator's dilemma, Wayne believes the giants will indeed continue to dominate the high-end interceptor market, but the low-end and middle solutions have already gone to five companies that received DoD contracts: Coaspire, Leidos, Anduril, Zone 5, and Castilian. The DoD wants tens of thousands of units, not an increase from 620 to 2,000. So in the short term, the giants have the advantage, but within three to five years, upstarts like Anduril could capture the middle market. This also means that when investing in defense stocks, you can't just look at traditional giants; you need to see who benefits from the procurement shift.

points.h: AI killer robots are still far off
points.body: Wayne says that in the Pentagon, AI is currently used only for intelligence analysis, image labeling for analysts, and change detection, not for strike decisions. His previous research at the war college was on 'AI and levels of trust.' Between target identification and tactical strike, it remains fully 'human-on-the-loop'—AI can help you find targets and issue alerts, but the final decision is still made by human commanders and intelligence analysts. Some worry that AI will decide on its own to destroy targets, but Wayne says that future is still a long way off. The risk models aren't ready, so the Pentagon currently does not use AI for autonomous killing; instead, it uses AI for military intelligence screening to replace tedious work.
